0.0.n: A fixed polite greeting used by staff welcoming customers.

1.0.n: This borrowed noun names the service the guest is requesting.

1.2.n: お願いします politely requests the service named just before it.

2.0.n: The prefix お adds respect when referring to the guest’s name.

2.2.n: From 伺う, a humble way to ask; お伺いします shows respect to the guest.

2.3.n: The polite form of する completes お伺いします, making the inquiry formal.

3.0.n: This is the guest’s family name, identified as Lin in the translation.

3.1.n: This polite ending identifies the speaker; the Japanese leaves out I.

4.0.n: 林 is the guest’s family name; 様 is a highly respectful title that does not specify gender.

4.1.n: This polite ending follows the guest’s name as the clerk confirms their identity.

4.2.n: This ending seeks confirmation of the guest’s name.

4.4.n: A formal expression for a short time, commonly used in customer service.

4.5.n: お plus the stem of 待つ combines with ください to make a respectful request.

4.6.n: After お待ち, this completes the polite request for the guest to wait.

5.0.n: The clerk uses this polite acknowledgment before checking the booking details.

5.2.n: 林 is the guest’s family name; 様 addresses the guest with high respect, without specifying gender.

5.4.n: This describes accommodation without meals included.

5.5.n: This borrowed word refers to the hotel’s booking package.

5.6.n: Links 素泊まりプラン to お部屋, identifying the room’s booking package.

5.7.n: The prefix お makes the reference to the guest’s room more polite.

5.9.n: 泊 counts overnight stays rather than days.

5.10.n: Marks three nights as the booking detail being checked.

5.11.n: The prefix お adds politeness; the clerk asks whether any booking detail is incorrect.

5.12.n: This is the stem of ございます, a very polite equivalent of あります, used here in the negative.

5.13.n: This is the part of ます used before ん to form the polite negative ending ません.

5.14.n: Completes ません; ございません politely says there is no mistake.

5.15.n: Turns the negative statement into a formal question confirming the booking details.

6.0.n: The guest politely agrees with the clerk’s confirmation question.

6.2.n: Refers back to the details the clerk just stated.

6.3.n: Adds politeness to そう, forming a standard expression of agreement.

7.0.n: The clerk acknowledges the guest’s confirmation before continuing.

7.2.n: Combines with ございます to express thanks politely.

7.3.n: This stem of ございます helps make ありがとう formal; it has no separate natural English translation here.

7.4.n: Completes ございます, giving the expression of thanks a polite ending.

7.6.n: This borrowed noun names the document the clerk wants to copy.

7.7.n: Marks the passport as the thing to be copied.

7.8.n: コピーする becomes コピーさせていただく, humbly receiving permission to copy; its て-form connects to も.

7.9.n: After the verb’s て-form, も combines with よろしい to ask whether the action is permitted.

7.10.n: よろしい is a polite alternative to いい; でしょう makes the permission request more tentative.

7.11.n: Completes the formal question asking the guest’s permission.

8.0.n: Here the guest politely grants permission to copy the passport.

0.tip: いらっしゃいませ is a standard customer greeting, not an everyday greeting between friends.

1.tip: A service name followed by お願いします is a useful way to make a polite request.

2.tip: お伺いします is a respectful way for staff to ask a guest for information.

3.tip: Japanese often leaves out I when the speaker’s identity is clear.

4.lit: You are Lin, right? Please wait a moment.
4.tip: お plus a verb stem plus ください makes a respectful request, as in お待ちください.

5.lit: Yes, Ms. Lin, room-only plan’s room, for three nights, is there no mistake?
5.tip: お間違いございませんか is a very polite way to check that details are correct.

6.tip: そうです confirms that what the other person said is correct.

7.lit: Yes, thank you. Would it be all right if I were allowed to copy the passport?
7.tip: させていただいてもよろしいでしょうか is a very formal, humble way to ask permission to do something.

8.tip: はい can grant permission, as it does in response to this request.
